newsitem.title: GERMANY: SECOND ESTIMATE OF EUROPEAN BEET SUGAR PRODUCTION.
newsitem.headline: SECOND ESTIMATE OF EUROPEAN BEET SUGAR PRODUCTION.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistican F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
SECOND ESTIMATE OF EUROPEAN BEET SUGAR PRODUCTION
(First figure 1996/97, second figure 1995/96, figures in brackets first estimate, 28 August 1996. All figures in 1000 tonnes, raw value.)

A mild autumn in Western Europe and an absence of severe frosts in Eastern Europe have improved the continent's sugar production prospects. Total output is now put at 29.4 million tonnes or about 800,000 tonnes up on the year. West Europe is expected to produce about 20.1 million tonnes, raw value, one million tonnes more than forecast in our first estimate and 1.2 million tonnes above the revised figure for 1995/96. Production in the EU is put at 17.395 million tonnes, or 392,000 tonnes above output in 1995/96, while in the three countries outside the EU - Turkey, ex-Yugoslavia and Switzerland - production will also be considerably higher. In East Europe, though the forecast total of 9.3 million tonnes is still about 400,000 tonnes below the revised figure for last year, it is likely to be about half a million tonnes more than was originally expected.

Ukraine is the largest producer in East Europe and official sources are estimating an output of more than 3.0 million tonnes, in raw value terms. Though recent weather conditions have favoured the crop we think this is too high and are currently estimating 2.93 million tonnes, raw value. In addition to its beet sugar industry the Ukraine also processes imported cane raws and current plans are for something in excess of 0.5 million tonnes of white sugar to be produced from imported raws. Russia is expected to produce no more than 1.80 million tonnes which with consumption needs of more than 5.0 million tonnes points to an import need of more than 3.0 million tonnes. A large proportion of this will be forthcoming from the Ukraine though to protect the Russian domestic industry an import quota of 1.5 million tonnes of white sugar has been set with a limit of 1.15 million tonnes from the Ukraine. Can EU sugar also find an outlet in Russia within this quota?

In addition to the imports from the Ukraine, Russian sources expect imports from Cuba to amount to more than one million tonnes of cane raws. Brazilian, Indian and Thai sugar are all in plentiful supply while some of the East Europeans have significant surpluses this year. In particular the Polish crop has reached a bumper 2.4 million tonnes this year, up from 1.7 million tonnes in 1995/96, which leaves a surplus in the region of 640,000 tonnes. Whether all of this would become available for export is doubtful as subsidised export quotas have been set at 133,000 tonnes, raw value in 1996 and 128,000 tonnes in 1997. Even so there would appear to be little opportunity for high quality EU white sugar to find much of an outlet in Russia.

It is interesting to note that Polish sugar, for which a maximum colour of 60 ICUMSA is guaranteed, has been delivered on both the London and the Paris future markets. As the EU guarantees a maximum colour of 45 ICUMSA it now commands a premium against the futures.

With white sugar in plentiful supply, particularly in view of the fact that new refineries in the Middle East will be operating, there may be problems in disposing of the higher crop expected in the EU, especially as there is expected to be a fall in demand for white sugar. Already the white sugar premium has been depressed and this may be forced down further in the next few months.

Probably more sugar will be carried over from the current EU crop than had been originally anticipated. That, in turn, could lead to lower sowings in 1997. Meanwhile protectionist measures by the Russian government may lead to reduced imports from the Ukraine and that, too, could lead to lower sowings. Whether such steps would result in a lower sugar output is another matter in view of the fact that the weather has not been particularly kind to beet growers this year.
